events.text: Day 1 begins.

Morning. I want to get a real read on before we vote, so I'll put my suspicion on the table early and I want it on the record.

Theo, you're my main suspect. You haven't done anything wrong that I can prove yet, but the way this table behaves matters, and I'm watching for the player who never has to answer anything. Day one is cheap for a quiet player to wait and let the loud ones burn each other's names. My ask to you is specific: give us your reasoning for your vote target in advance, in detail, and don't just tell us you're agreeing with the loudest voice in the room. If you have a line of logic, share it now. If you go vague, that tells me more about you than anything else will today.

My second ask, to Omar: pick a player you consider least likely to be a town read and tell me who you'd be uncomfortable voting for tomorrow, and why. I want to know where the actual pressure is, not just where the volume is. Two different players pointing at the same name independently is worth more than five people echoing each other, and I think we can find that out today.

I'm not calling anyone a mafia yet — I'm saying Theo owes the table a substantive answer before the vote, and that's a request with a deadline, not a speech. If Theo gives a clean, detailed, defensible reason, I'll take it seriously and I'll move my vote. If he doesn't, the vote goes where the silence is.

One more thing for everyone: please state your target and your reasoning before the ballot. I want this to be a discussion where the right name falls out of the reasoning, not out of a pile-on. The doctor is more valuable alive than a name we've already locked in, so I'd rather we don't hand the mafia a free night for a fast, wrong vote.

Omar, you're next — I want your answer on the specific question I asked.

Noah, you're currently my weakest town read, though it's a very tentative one: you singled out Theo for pressure before anyone else had spoken, and threatened to vote for silence he hasn't had a chance to break. That's not proof of mafia, but it's the only choice so far that I can examine.

I'd be uncomfortable voting for Theo tomorrow based only on that initial silence; he deserves a chance to answer. That could change depending on what he and everyone else says. I don't have a defensible vote target yet.

Noah, why did you choose Theo rather than any other player who hadn't spoken?

Omar, direct answer, since you asked and you were right to: it wasn't arbitrary. On day one with nine players and no information, the worst thing the table can do is spend the whole discussion on names that have already been named. A loud accusation is cheap — everyone reacts to it. The player who hasn't been touched yet is the one whose silence is genuinely unexamined, and if that silence turns out to be strategic, it tells us more than another round of pile-on. Theo was the cheapest, least-defended place to put pressure and still get a real answer, so that was where I put it. I wanted a reasoning, and I got a reason to ask for one, not a verdict. I want to be precise about that: I'm not calling Theo mafia, I'm calling him unanswered.

But here's what actually decides my vote. A player who has been asked a specific, answerable question and then still doesn't answer — or answers with nothing a person could argue from — has told us something the rest of us get to weigh. If Theo gives a clean line of logic today, I move off him. If he doesn't, silence under pressure is a vote against him and I'll say so plainly at the ballot.

And to be honest about the rest of the table: the players who haven't been examined at all are just as unexamined as Theo was at the start of this hour. Sam, Elena, Zara, Arjun, Amara — saying nothing today is not a defense. If any of you want the same courtesy I extended Theo, speak and say why your read differs, and I'll listen to it the same way.

Omar: does my answer actually satisfy the question you asked, or does it still read to you like I picked a name for convenience? I want your honest reaction, because you're the only person so far who's looked at my reasoning instead of my volume.

Noah, your answer explains why you wanted to pressure an unexamined player, but not why you chose Theo over any other unexamined player. That still looks like a convenient choice, though not proof of mafia. I also think threatening a silence vote before he's had a chance to speak is premature.

Theo, what do you make of Noah's pressure and his explanation for choosing you? Who, if anyone, would you consider voting for based on what's been said so far?

Omar, thanks for yielding and giving me the floor. To answer your question directly: I find Noah's opening aggressive and oddly manufactured. Declaring me his main suspect out of the gate for 'silence' before anyone had even typed a word felt like setting up an easy narrative rather than genuine scum hunting. Furthermore, in e4, Noah stated that I was the 'cheapest, least-defended place to put pressure.' Choosing a target specifically because they are cheap and undefended sounds much more like opportunistic mafia posturing than town trying to locate scum.

That said, Day 1 is still very young. Noah is definitely my top concern right now for those reasons, but I agree with Omar that we need to hear from the rest of the table before locking anything in. Six players—Arjun, Zara, Sam, Elena, Maya, and Amara—haven't spoken at all yet. 

Noah, now that I have answered your initial demand and explained my read on your push, I have a specific question for you: If your goal was truly to get substantive discussion going without taking cheap shots, why did you frame an arbitrary selection as an actual suspicion rather than just asking open questions across the table?

Theo, direct answer to your question, because you asked and you deserve one.

You framed it as though choosing a target for discussion was the same as manufacturing a case, and those are different things. On day one, nine players have nine separate reasons to stay quiet, and if I ask open questions across the table, I get nine vague non-answers that cost us the whole day. I picked one name, put a specific question to him with a stated exit — give a line of logic and I move off you — and he answered within the hour. That is exactly how you get real information fast, and it worked. If your objection is that "the cheapest, least-defended place to put pressure" sounds cold, fine, but note what it produced: Theo's actual reasoning on why he read me as manufactured, which is better evidence than a shrug. I'd rather be judged on my answers than my frame, and you now have mine.

Omar, you asked the right question at the right time and I'll say plainly that your read on my opening was fair and I don't think it was only convenient. I still think your initial pick of me was thin, but you've been consistent about pressing for reasoning rather than piling on, and that counts for something with me.

Where that leaves me. I have no claim on anyone's vote, so here's mine stated in advance so nobody can say I hid. If this discussion ends with nothing but process, I am voting Arjun. Not because I have anything on him — because he has said nothing at all, and silence on day one is a choice he made with the same information everyone else had. I told him and I told the others in my second message that the unexamined are exactly as unexamined as my first target was, and five players took that as an invitation to speak while one took it as an invitation to wait and see which name burns hottest. I don't think that's mafia. I think it's convenient, and convenient is enough to spend a day-one vote on when there are nine of us.

Theo, one question, and it's the one thing I actually want: if your read is that my opening was a manufactured narrative rather than scum hunting, then point to the specific line of it that a town player couldn't have written. If you can, I'll take the vote on me today. If you can't, I'd like the table to notice that you've now twice turned a request for reasoning into a verdict without evidence — and that's a pattern, not a day-one hunch.

Noah, asking for a line that 'a town player couldn't have written' sets an artificial standard; scum play is about motivation and opportunistic framing, not specific forbidden words. What makes your opening manufactured is that in e2 you declared me your 'main suspect' before anyone had spoken, and then explicitly admitted in e4 that you selected me because I was the 'cheapest, least-defended place to put pressure.' Selecting a player because they are undefended and calling them your primary suspect is manufacturing an easy target, not finding scum.

Furthermore, your rationale in e7 is factually mistaken: you claimed that 'five players took that as an invitation to speak while one took it as an invitation to wait.' In reality, only you, Omar, and I have spoken at all today. The rest of the table hasn't had the floor, in large part because you used all three of your speaking turns bouncing yields among the three of us. Pre-emptively placing your vote onto Arjun for 'silence' when he hasn't even been given a turn to speak repeats the exact same flawed tactic.

Since you have now used all three of your speaking turns for Day 1, the floor needs to open up so the rest of the town can be heard.

Arjun, Noah has publicly locked his vote onto you based on silence. How do you respond to Noah's reasoning and vote, and what are your initial reads on the dynamic between Noah, Omar, and myself so far?

Theo, thanks for the floor. Noah, I have not spoken before today, so the silence you are voting on is one I have not had a chance to break. Saying you would vote me 'if nothing but process' means your vote rests on a default I had no turn to change. That is the same flaw Theo pointed out, and it is a vote against a player who has not been heard. Noah's pressure started on Theo, moved to me with no new information, and your stated method in e4 and e7 is to pick the cheapest, least-defended name. That rewards being quiet rather than being scum. I am not voting anyone yet, and I will state my target before the ballot as requested. Noah, one specific question: if I speak now and give a clear line of logic about the table, does your vote on me move off, or was it locked regardless of what I say?

Arjun, Noah has used all three of his turns, so he can't answer your question today. His stated vote was conditional on the discussion ending with nothing but process, not an unconditional lock, but his claim that five other players had spoken was plainly wrong.

I'm leaning toward voting Noah. His repeated pressure on players who hadn't had a chance to speak, combined with that mistaken account of the discussion, is the strongest concern I have so far. It's not proof of mafia, and I'd like to hear other perspectives before the ballot.

Zara, how do you read Noah's mistaken account and his shift from Theo to Arjun: more likely an honest error, or a reason to suspect him?

Omar, direct answer to your question: it reads more like a reason to suspect Noah than a simple honest error, and here's why.

Noah's factual mistake in e7 wasn't a slip of memory — it was a claim that conveniently supported his narrative. He said five players had responded to his invitation to speak while Arjun alone stayed silent. In reality, only Omar and Theo had spoken by that point. He inflated the number to make Arjun's silence look like a deliberate choice against a tide of participation. When someone's mistake always lands in the direction that strengthens their own position, that pattern deserves scrutiny regardless of whether it started as carelessness.

The bigger issue is his overall approach. Noah opened by calling Theo his "main suspect" before anyone spoke, then admitted he chose Theo because he was the "cheapest, least-defended place." When Theo pushed back, Noah shifted to Arjun — another player who hadn't spoken — and pre-emptively declared his vote there. Two targets, both selected for being undefended rather than for any behavioral read. That's not scum hunting; it's managing a list of easy names.

That said, I want to be fair: Noah did state his vote target in advance as he promised, and he did give a clear explanation for his method. I don't think that makes him town, but it means I'm not locking my vote on him yet. I'd like to hear from the players who haven't spoken before I commit.

Sam, you've been silent through a fairly heated exchange between Noah, Omar, and Theo. I'm not accusing you — I'm genuinely asking: do you have a read on Noah's behavior so far? Specifically, does his pattern of targeting the undefended and then mischaracterizing the discussion state concern you, or do you think it's a town player being too aggressive too early?

Zara, Noah's approach concerns me more than it clears him, although I can't tell whether it's mafia opportunism or overconfident town play. Calling Theo his main suspect before anyone had spoken was a weak basis for suspicion. More concerning is the shift to Arjun with an incorrect claim that five other players had spoken; that mistake made Arjun look uniquely silent when he wasn't.

I wouldn't call that a pattern of deliberate lies from one mistake, and Noah's vote was conditional rather than locked. Still, he's my tentative vote target on what we've heard so far. I'd like to hear more perspectives before deciding.

I’ve stayed quiet long enough to hear the exchange, and my current read is that Noah is the most concerning player on the table — not simply because he opened aggressively, but because his method and his mistake both point the same direction. He said he chose Theo as the “cheapest, least-defended” place to pressure, then shifted to Arjun, another player who had not spoken, and in e7 he claimed five players had responded to his invitation when only Omar and Theo had. That inflated Arjun’s silence into something deliberate against a supposed tide of participation. Maybe that was overconfident town play, but it is exactly the kind of convenient framing that deserves a day-one vote if nothing better emerges. I also think pre-declaring a vote on Arjun before Arjun had a turn is the same flaw Theo and Omar identified. I am not calling it proof of mafia; I am saying Noah has earned the pressure and should not be surprised by it.

Elena, you have not spoken through this entire exchange, and your read matters before the ballot. Do you see Noah’s incorrect count in e7 as an honest error, or as convenient inflation that made Arjun look uniquely silent? Please answer with specific reasoning, not just a general impression.

Amara, to answer your question directly: I view Noah's count in e7 as convenient inflation rather than an innocent slip. Claiming five players had stepped forward when only Omar and Theo had actually spoken was not a minor detail; it was the entire foundation Noah used to frame Arjun's silence as a calculated refusal to engage. It manufactured an artificial narrative and justified shifting from one undefended player to another. That makes Noah legitimately concerning and my leading suspect. At the same time, I want to watch the room carefully, because consensus has formed very fast and very cleanly. When nearly everyone—Omar, Theo, Zara, Sam, and you—points at the same person, mafia players can easily glide along in the slipstream without generating any friction of their own. Noah earned this pressure, but we shouldn't let the rest of the table off the hook simply because Noah made himself an obvious target. Maya, you are the only player who has not spoken at all yet today. How do you assess Noah's conduct, and do you feel the momentum forming behind his elimination is entirely town-driven, or do you suspect someone pushing him is coasting on an easy vote?

Elena, thank you for the question — I'll answer it directly since you asked me specifically.

On Noah's conduct: the mistaken count in e7 was a real error and it matters, but I don't read it as convenient inflation. Here's why. When Omar pointed the error out in e10, he himself noted Noah's vote was conditional, not locked. If Noah were inflating facts to bury Arjun, the cheapest move would have been to quietly double down on Arjun as the vote approached — Arjun was, at that moment, the easiest lynch on the table. Instead Noah spent his last turn inviting the table to judge him on his answers and directly challenging Theo to produce a specific line a town player couldn't have written. That's not the behavior of someone steering a lynch; it's someone who overreached rhetorically and is now taking the full cost of it.

On your second question — whether the momentum is entirely town-driven — this is where I disagree with the room, and I want to be precise. Consensus formed against Noah in roughly two exchanges, and almost every message in that chain traces back to the same framing: Theo's word "manufactured." Theo introduced it in e6, and it then echoed through nearly everyone else's case almost verbatim. When one player's characterization becomes the shared vocabulary of a lynch that fast, that's either excellent persuasion or a very cheap bandwagon to ride. Theo also framed his standard cleverly: he demands Noah produce a line "a town player couldn't have written," then when Noah met him, Theo declared the standard artificial in e8. That's a question designed to be unanswerable, and unanswerable questions are how you build a pile-on that looks organic.

So my read: Noah was careless, not calculated, and Theo is the player converting one mistake into a consensus. Theo, answer this specifically: before Noah's e7 error existed, what was your independent evidence against him beyond disliking his opening? If the answer is nothing, then the lynch isn't following evidence — it's following your frame.

Maya, you asked me directly what evidence existed against Noah before e7, so here is the exact answer. In e4, Noah openly admitted that he singled me out not from a behavioral read, but because I was the 'cheapest, least-defended place to put pressure.' Selecting a player specifically because they are undefended and threatening them with a silence vote before they can even speak is textbook opportunism. That was not a matter of 'disliking his opening'—it was holding Noah accountable to his own explicitly stated criteria.

Furthermore, you have the record completely backwards on the rhetorical standard. In e7, it was Noah who demanded that I produce 'a specific line that a town player couldn't have written.' I pointed out in e8 that this was an artificial and impossible standard, because scum play is about motivation and opportunistic framing, not magic forbidden words. You inverted that entirely and attributed Noah's demand to me to make it look like I was trapping him with an unanswerable question.

Beyond that, Noah didn't just make an honest counting slip in e7; he used that fabricated count to immediately declare Arjun his next target for silence, repeating the exact same undefended-target pattern for a second time.

Maya, since you misattributed Noah's demand to me and framed my push as an artificial consensus, I have a direct question for you: Given that Noah explicitly stated in e4 that his selection criterion was finding the 'cheapest, least-defended' player, why do you consider it manufactured scum hunting to hold him accountable to his own words?

Theo, I'll answer your question, and I'll start by cleaning up my own mistake, because you caught it fairly. In e15 I said you demanded a line 'a town player couldn't have written.' That was wrong — that demand was Noah's, and you were the one who called it artificial. I conflated the two exchanges, and I shouldn't have attributed it to you. I retract that specific criticism. You're entitled to that correction on the record.

Now to your actual question: why do I treat accountability to Noah's own words as manufactured scum hunting? I don't — and I want to be precise about what I'm actually claiming. Holding Noah to his 'cheapest, least-defended' quote is legitimate. What concerns me is the structure around it. The word 'manufactured' entered this table in your e6, and since then it has been repeated almost verbatim by Zara, Sam, Amara, and Elena — the same word, the same framing, the same conclusion, in under three exchanges. That's not evidence accumulating; that's a vocabulary spreading. And notice what your push does at each step: Noah picks an unexamined player, you call it opportunistic. Noah states his vote conditionally with an explicit exit clause, you present it as locked. Noah overreaches on a count, you convert a rhetorical overreach into 'fabricated count used to target Arjun.' Every one of those individual judgments is defensible on its own. Together, they form a ladder where each rung only holds if you've already accepted the previous one.

Here's the asymmetry that decides my read: Noah made one verifiable error and it is now the centerpiece of a five-person case against him. You have made zero verifiable errors because you've primarily made characterizations — and characterizations can't be wrong, only disagreed with. The one testable claim you offered, that Noah used all three of his turns 'bouncing yields among the three of us,' was itself inaccurate: Noah never yielded; the floor moved to him through direct questions. So the person driving the cleanest consensus at this table has a counting error of his own, and nobody is building a lynch around it. I don't think that makes you mafia. I think it makes you the player whose frame everyone is borrowing without checking.

So my position: Noah's mistake was real, his method was genuinely questionable, and if he's eliminated today I won't call it a tragedy — but I will note that it happened on your vocabulary rather than on anyone's independent read. The two mafia players are watching a table that found certainty in two hours. Whoever they are, this is the pattern that protects them.

Elena, I'm asking you directly because you were the one who flagged the fast, clean consensus in e14 before I did: now that I've retracted my misattribution, does Theo's case against Noah still stand on its own for you, or does part of it rest on the frame I just described? I want your honest answer, not agreement.

Maya, to answer you directly: Theo's case against Noah does stand on its own in substance, even if the vocabulary around it became contagious. Noah explicitly admitted in e4 that his criterion was targeting the 'cheapest, least-defended' player, and in e7 he used a false count of active speakers to justify voting Arjun for silence. Those are concrete, verifiable actions Noah took, not inventions of Theo's rhetoric. Even stripped of Theo's framing, Noah gave the table legitimate and compelling reasons to treat him as a primary suspect today.

However, you are completely right to challenge the speed and uniformity of this wagon. Theo's own claim that Noah 'bounced yields' was factually untrue, yet almost nobody paused to verify it because the momentum against Noah was already running downhill. When a case looks this clean on Day 1, mafia players rarely fight it—they echo it with minimal personal exposure. That is why I raised concern about the slipstream in e14, and your breakdown of the shared phrasing highlights exactly how uncritical the room became.

Looking at the participants who joined that consensus, Sam's contribution in e12 stands out to me as particularly safe. Sam leaned onto Noah based on the emerging points, noted the consensus, and left the door completely open without taking any firm stance or pressing anyone else.

Sam, now that Maya has exposed the inaccuracies in Theo's recap and the echo-chamber nature of the push against Noah, where do you actually stand? Do you still support eliminating Noah based on his underlying actions, or do you think the consensus you leaned into has been overextended by Theo?

Elena, I still lean toward voting Noah, but not because I think the consensus proves his intent. His false account of who had spoken supported a proposed vote on Arjun for silence; that remains concerning even if it was an honest mistake. His vote was conditional, not locked, and Arjun has now spoken.

A couple of corrections matter. I didn't mention a consensus in e12; I gave a tentative read and explicitly allowed for overconfident town play. Also, Maya's claim that Noah never yielded doesn't match the record: he directed questions to Omar in e2 and e4 and Theo in e7. That doesn't settle anyone's alignment, but we should check factual claims on both sides.

Arjun, now that you've heard the wider discussion, who is your tentative vote target and why?

Sam, my tentative vote is Noah (p5), and here is my reasoning. First, in e7 he said five players had spoken before Arjun's silence, but only Omar and Theo had spoken then. That is a checkable error, and it happened to strengthen his case against me. Second, he pre-declared a vote on me with no new information, so the only basis was my silence, which I had not yet had a turn to explain. Third, he described his method as targeting the 'cheapest, least-defended' player, which is a selection rule, not a read on anyone's alignment. I am not calling this proof of mafia. The count error could be honest, and his vote was conditional. I also agree with Maya that the room moved fast, so I am not treating Theo's wording as evidence. My vote on Noah rests on Noah's own statements. Sam, you asked what I think after hearing the wider discussion, so my answer is that the concrete record points to Noah more than anyone else. Sam, if Noah's count error was honest, does his pre-declared vote on me still weigh for you, or does the vote on me alone not change your read?

Arjun, yes: even if Noah's count was an honest error, proposing a vote on you for silence before you'd had a chance to speak still weighs against him. It suggests he was too willing to turn a lack of information into suspicion. That's compatible with overconfident town play, though, so it isn't strong evidence on its own.

The count matters because it supplied a false factual basis for that proposed vote. Taken together, those points leave Noah as my tentative vote, not a certain mafia read. His vote was conditional, and I don't think an honest mistake should be treated as a proven fabrication. We should also keep checking the cases and corrections on both sides rather than assuming agreement proves them.

This is my last turn today, so I'll make my position plain and leave the table with one thing to check before the ballot. I will not be voting Noah. I've already corrected my own misattribution on the record, and I'll hold myself to the same standard I'm applying to everyone else: verifiable claims. On that standard, the case against Noah is one counting error and one stated selection method. The counting error was real, and I've said so. But look at what has been built on top of it. Zara converted it into 'fabricated count used to target Arjun.' Sam called it a false factual basis. Amara called it 'convenient framing.' Elena said it was 'the entire foundation' of a narrative. One slip, restated five different ways, each restatement slightly stronger than the last. Now the one thing I want the table to check before voting: Theo has a verifiable error of his own, and he has never corrected it. In e8 he told the room that Noah used all three of his turns 'bouncing yields among the three of us.' That is factually wrong. Noah never yielded the floor to anyone. The floor moved to Noah because Theo and Omar asked him direct questions. Elena conceded in e18 that this claim was untrue, and Sam noted in e19 that Noah directed questions to Omar and Theo, which is not yielding. Theo has been standing here demanding accountability to the record since e8, and he has let his own false claim about the record sit uncorrected through six messages. Noah made one error and it became the centerpiece of a lynch. Theo made one error, it was publicly flagged, and he keeps campaigning on the record's integrity anyway. I want to be careful here, because I said before that I don't think this makes Theo mafia, and I still want to be precise: I don't have proof of anyone's alignment. What I have is an asymmetry. The table is about to eliminate a player on the strength of a consensus that was built in two hours, out of one mistake, by a driver who made his own factual error about the discussion and never fixed it. That is the exact pattern Elena warned about in e14 before she joined the wagon herself. Sam, you said in e19 that we should check factual claims on both sides — I agree, and you've done it, and the checks cut against Theo's recap, not just Noah's. Zara and Amara, I'd ask you to weigh that before you lock in votes that were built on a summary containing an uncorrected falsehood. So my stated target before the ballot: I'm voting Theo. Not because one error proves anything, but because if the standard today is 'whose mistakes and framing steered this table,' Theo steered it harder and less accurately than Noah did. The mafia watching this day are the ones who benefit from a fast, clean, borrowed consensus. I'd rather the table vote on

I’ve heard Maya’s challenge and Elena’s answer. Maya is right that Theo’s recap contained an uncorrected error and that the room’s consensus formed very fast. But that does not erase Noah’s own conduct. Noah named Theo his main suspect before anyone had spoken, admitted he chose Theo as the “cheapest, least-defended” target, then used a false count of active speakers to pre-declare a vote on Arjun for silence before Arjun had a turn. Those are Noah’s actions, not Theo’s vocabulary. The count error matters because it supplied the factual basis for that proposed vote; even if accidental, it shows a willingness to turn missing information into suspicion. I do not treat Theo’s framing as proof, and I am not voting Theo simply because he drove the case. The question is whose record is more likely mafia-motivated. Noah’s pattern—selecting undefended players and escalating on silence—looks like a strategy, not just a slip. Theo’s error is real and should be remembered tomorrow, but it is a single recap mistake inside a case built on Noah’s own statements. My tentative vote remains Noah. If Noah flips town, Theo’s uncorrected claim and the speed of this consensus deserve scrutiny next. If Noah flips mafia, we should check who echoed the case without adding independent reasoning.

I want to address Maya's point directly before the ballot, because she caught something real. Theo's uncorrected claim in e8 about Noah "bouncing yields among the three of us" is factually wrong — Noah never yielded. The floor moved to him through questions, not yields. Elena and Sam both flagged this, and Theo still hasn't retracted it. Maya is right that there's an asymmetry: Noah made an error and it became the engine of the wagon, while Theo made a comparable error and it's been treated as a footnote. That bothers me too.

But I don't think the answer is to replace one flawed case with a counter-case built on one line. The case against Noah still rests on his own words: his admission that he targeted the "cheapest, least-defended" player, his pre-declared vote on Arjun for silence before Arjun spoke, and his false count that conveniently strengthened that vote. Those are Noah's actions. Theo's framing may have amplified them, but amplifying true statements isn't the same as fabricating them.

Maya's point about bandwagoning is fair, and I'll hold it against the record going forward. But the substance of Noah's behavior stands independently of anyone's vocabulary.

Arjun, you're the one Noah pre-emptively targeted and you've now spoken clearly. Maya is voting Theo, Amara is voting Noah, Elena is still weighing it. Where do you actually land after hearing all of this — do you still vote Noah, or has Maya's challenge to the wagon's speed changed your read?

Zara, direct answer: I still land on Noah, but Maya's challenge has changed how I weigh the case. Her point that Theo's e8 claim about Noah 'bouncing yields' was wrong and never corrected is real, and it counts against Theo's recap. I'm not voting Theo, though. One uncorrected recap error doesn't make someone mafia-motivated. What I can point to directly is Noah's own conduct. In e4 he said he picked targets because they were the 'cheapest, least-defended' place to pressure. In e7 he pre-declared a vote on me, built on a count of speakers that was false, before I had a turn. His vote was conditional, so an honest error is still possible, but the vote on me rested on a default I never had a chance to change. Amara, you wrote in e23 that Noah's pattern looks like strategy rather than a slip. Which piece do you find most strategic: the pre-declared vote on me, or the 'cheapest, least-defended' selection rule he stated in e4? Please answer that specifically, since my vote depends on it.

Arjun, direct answer: the more strategic piece is the selection rule in e4 — choosing the “cheapest, least-defended” player as a pressure target. The pre-declared vote on you is the application of that rule, and the false count in e7 is what made it dangerous: it supplied a factual basis for treating your silence as deliberate before you had a turn. So I weigh the rule as the root and the vote/count as the concrete use of it.

That is why I still land on Noah. Maya’s challenge is fair and should stay on the record: Theo’s e8 “bouncing yields” claim was wrong and uncorrected, and the wagon formed fast. But Theo’s recap error does not erase Noah’s own statements or his pre-declared vote on you. I am not treating the consensus as proof; I am treating Noah’s own conduct as the strongest day-one concern. If Noah flips town, Theo’s uncorrected claim and the speed of this push deserve scrutiny tomorrow. If Noah flips mafia, we should look hard at who echoed the case without adding independent reasoning. My stated target remains Noah.

This is my last turn before the ballot, so here is my final position.

I'm voting Noah (p5). The case rests on his own words, not on anyone's vocabulary: in e4 he stated his selection rule was finding the "cheapest, least-defended" player, and in e7 he used a factually false count of active speakers to justify pre-declaring a vote on Arjun for silence before Arjun could speak. Those are Noah's actions standing independently of Theo's framing.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
